opus-5.5.text:
I wouldn't say it's entirely wrong. Language is incredibly useful, and the progress we've gotten from vision-language models has been real. But I think treating language as the *foundation* for robotics gets the order of things backwards.

Think about how intelligence developed in nature. Animals were manipulating objects, navigating complex terrain, using tools, long before anything like language existed. A squirrel or a crow has remarkable physical intelligence and no language at all. Even for a human child, a lot of the core understanding of the physical world, like object permanence, how things fall, how much force you need to pick something up without crushing it, comes before they can describe any of it in words. Language sits on top of that physical grounding. It doesn't create it.

The issue with building robot systems mainly on language models is that language is a very lossy, compressed description of the physical world. I can tell you "pick up the cup," but that sentence carries almost nothing about the contact dynamics, the friction, the subtle wrist adjustment when the cup is fuller than you expected. That information is the hard part of manipulation, and it simply isn't in internet text. So when you start from a language backbone and try to attach actions to it, you get a system that's very good at high-level reasoning, like planning steps or knowing that the sponge goes near the sink, but still struggles with the low-level physical interaction that makes up most of the real difficulty.

There's also a data side to this. The reason language became the foundation in AI generally is that we had a huge amount of text. That's a historical accident of what data was available, not proof that language is the right representation for embodied intelligence. If we let data availability decide our architecture, we may end up optimizing for the wrong thing.

So my view is that the foundation should be something closer to a model of physical interaction: understanding dynamics, contact, and how actions change the world, learned from rich sensorimotor data like vision, touch, and proprioception, and from things like human videos and demonstrations. Language then becomes an interface. It's a very good way to specify goals and to communicate with people, and it can help with abstract reasoning, but it shouldn't be the core everything else is built around.

r001.rationale: The response says language is a lossy description that omits contact dynamics and other details of physical interaction, placing language-based control too far from the physical layer.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I'd push back a little on the framing first, because I don't think language is wrong as a capability. It's incredibly useful as an interface. When a person wants to tell a robot what to do, language is the most natural channel we have. My concern is with putting it at the foundation, as the thing everything else gets built on top of.

Here's the core issue. Language is a compression of human experience, and it's a lossy compression that's tuned for communication between agents who already share a body and a world. When I say "put the mug on the shelf," I'm leaving out almost everything that actually matters for doing it. How heavy the mug is, whether it's full, where my fingers need to go so I don't crush it, how the shelf is going to shift when I set something on it. None of that is in the sentence. It's in the physics. Humans don't need it spelled out because we've spent years touching things. A robot that learns primarily from text inherits the vocabulary without the grounding.

So the failure mode I see is a system that can talk fluently about the world but doesn't actually model it at the level that control requires. Language models are great at the "what" and often at the "why," but manipulation lives in the "how," at millisecond timescales, in continuous contact dynamics. That layer is pre-linguistic. Children manipulate objects skillfully long before they can describe what they're doing, and that's not a coincidence about development, it's a hint about where the hard part lives.

There's also a data argument. Internet text is enormous, and it's tempting to treat that as the free lunch that will carry robotics the way it carried NLP. But the text that exists almost never describes low-level motor behavior, because no human ever needed to write it down. The distribution we need for robot learning, embodied interaction with forces and outcomes, is exactly the distribution the internet is missing.

What I'd argue for instead is a foundation built around perception and action, around learning world models and skills from interaction, and then layering language on top as a way to specify goals, decompose tasks, and transfer common sense knowledge. Language as a steering wheel, not as the engine. If you get that ordering backward, you end up with very articulate robots that still fumble a cup of coffee, and I think we've already seen a bit of that.

r001.rationale: The response says language omits crucial physical details and lacks grounding in physics, while robot control depends on continuous contact dynamics. This communicates that language’s symbolic layer is too removed from the physical layer.

astra-6.text:
I wouldn’t say language is the wrong tool. I think the mistake is treating language as the foundation for everything a robot needs to understand. Language is how we describe the world, but it leaves out a lot of what matters when you physically interact with it.

If I tell a robot, “Pick up that cup,” the instruction is simple. But it doesn’t tell the robot how much force to apply, whether the cup is slippery, or how to adjust when it starts to slip. Those things require perception, action, and feedback. You need to learn from interacting with the world.

Language can be a powerful interface for expressing goals and bringing in general knowledge. But understanding what someone wants and knowing how to make it happen physically are different capabilities. I’d want language connected to a system grounded in perception and action, rather than assume that physical competence will emerge from language alone.

r001.rationale: The response says language describes the world but omits details needed for physical interaction, and that language must be connected to perception and action. This communicates that language-driven control is insufficiently grounded in the physical layer.

sol-6.1.text:
I wouldn’t say language is the wrong tool. I think the problem is treating language as the foundation of all intelligence. For a robot, the fundamental challenge is interacting with the physical world: understanding what’s happening, predicting how an action will change it, and adjusting when things don’t go as expected. Language can describe those things, but the description isn’t the capability itself.

You can tell a robot, “Pick up that cup,” and a language model can understand the instruction or break it into steps. But that doesn’t tell the robot exactly how to grasp the cup, how much force to use, or what to do when it starts slipping. Those abilities need to be grounded in perception and action.

So I see language as a very useful interface and a source of knowledge. But I don’t think we should assume that solving language automatically solves robotics. The robot also has to learn from interacting with the world.

r001.rationale: The response says language can describe actions but is not the physical capability itself, and that grasping, force control, and adapting to slipping require grounding in perception and action. This communicates the gap between language-driven symbolic control and physical interaction.
